raw_response:
For this rebuild, I would compare MediaManager with a modular Sonarr/Radarr plus Bazarr setup using the two requirements that matter most: obtaining the right subtitles for your foreign shows and reliably importing files from the seedbox. The sources below establish useful components for those jobs, but they do not demonstrate that a particular complete configuration has been deployed successfully for your collection.

## Ranked candidates

1. **Bazarr — subtitle management.** [Official setup guide](https://wiki.bazarr.media/Getting-Started/Setup-Guide/)  
   This is the most directly relevant component for the subtitle requirement. It documents language profiles, forced and hearing-impaired preferences, subtitle providers, and synchronization alongside Sonarr and Radarr. It needs access to the actual media files, and provider availability still determines which shows and languages are covered. The inspected guide is dated November 19, 2026, so its current instructions are later evidence than the January 8, 2026 question.

2. **MediaManager — the integrated option.** [Public repository](https://github.com/maxdorninger/MediaManager) · [Download-client documentation](https://maximilian-dorninger.gitbook.io/mediamanager/configuration/download-clients)  
   MediaManager offers TV and movie management in one interface. The client documentation describes qBittorrent, Transmission, and SABnzbd connections, but it also requires access to download directories; Transmission has an explicit same-path/same-volume requirement. I would therefore treat subtitle coverage and remote-file handling as acceptance tests before migration. These sources did not establish its complete foreign-subtitle workflow, and their relevant historical version dates remain unknown.

3. **Sonarr — television automation.** [Official site](https://sonarr.tv/)  
   Sonarr supplies series release selection, quality profiles, and failed-download handling. Its Docker guidance explicitly addresses consistent storage paths, permissions, and hardlinks, all relevant to retaining seeding while importing episodes. For a remote seedbox, arrange actual file access or transfer as part of the design. The live page supports these mechanisms, but I did not establish a dated version before the cutoff.

4. **SeedSync — the remote-transfer component.** [Public repository](https://github.com/ipsingh06/seedsync)  
   SeedSync runs locally and pulls files from a remote Linux server using SSH credentials and LFTP. Its pattern-based queuing and extraction can supply the missing transfer step between a seedbox and a home media server. It does not choose releases or manage subtitles, so it complements either management approach. Validate the handoff to your import process and continued seeding. The inspected README's historical availability is unverified.

5. **Radarr — the movie counterpart.** [Official site](https://radarr.video/)  
   If the collection also includes films, Radarr provides movie release selection, failed-download handling, and custom format prioritization. Its storage guidance has the same practical relevance as Sonarr's: download and library folders must be accessible with consistent paths and permissions. It adds another service and needs a subtitle component such as Bazarr. The verified page is live, with no reliable historical version date established.

6. **Medusa — an alternative integrated TV workflow.** [Official settings wiki](https://github.com/pymedusa/Medusa/wiki/Settings-explained) · [Seedbox integration guide](https://docs.seedboxes.cc/howtos/how-to-use-medusa-with-your-seedbox/)  
   Medusa combines television automation with built-in subtitle-language and provider settings. The seedbox guide describes subtitle searches and copying completed episodes while continuing to seed. This makes it a plausible third approach when reducing the number of TV-related services matters. It is TV-focused, and one provider's instructions do not prove universal seedbox compatibility. Both inspected guides carry dates before the cutoff: October 22 and September 17, 2025.

7. **Subgen — generated subtitles when providers cannot supply them.** [Public repository](https://github.com/McCloudS/subgen)  
   Subgen can produce subtitles from media audio and translate foreign speech into English, with a Bazarr integration. This addresses a different failure mode from downloading existing subtitles. It requires compute resources and a quality check on actual dialogue; arbitrary translation target languages are not established. The project's dated changelog records Bazarr support in October 2023 and language controls in December 2025. Current 2026 fixes should not be assumed available at the cutoff.

## How I would use this shortlist

My inference from the documented responsibilities is that interface consolidation alone will not settle the choice. Start with a representative foreign-language episode and an existing seedbox download. Check whether the intended subtitle language is found, whether timing is usable, whether the completed file becomes accessible to the manager, and whether importing preserves the intended seeding behavior. Repeat with a film only if films are in scope.

A modular candidate combines Sonarr for shows, Radarr if needed for movies, and Bazarr for subtitles; SeedSync is an optional transfer component when files must move from the seedbox to the local server. MediaManager deserves the same small acceptance trial because it could simplify management, while the inspected evidence leaves its subtitle and remote-storage fit unresolved. Medusa is a narrower TV alternative, and Subgen is a fallback mechanism for missing subtitle files.

This is a discovery shortlist, not a migration success claim or a finding that one application is universally better.
